archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, defense-reliant)
archetype.definition: A team still digging out of back-to-back bottom-tier seasons, leaning on a conservative run-heavy plan and a sound tackling defense to stay close while the passing game remains the league's least productive.

report.headline: Closer than 1-6 looks, but the offense still can't carry a game.
report.take:
The Titans are a team that plays to keep games small. Their pass rate over expected of -9.4 ranks 30th, they are aggressive on fourth down, they commit few penalties, and they have mostly stayed within a score of better teams. Cam Ward has started every game behind a line that protects well. Its QB-hit rate ranks 4th and its sack rate 8th. That has not translated into offense. The unit ranks 31st in EPA per play and last in yards per game, so the problem is not the pocket. The passing game simply isn't producing, and with Tony Pollard taking nearly all the carries, the run game is steady but not explosive enough to make up the gap.

The record overstates how bad they are, but only a little. They have a .200 win rate in one-score games and sit 1.4 wins below what the point differential implies. The differential itself says 2.4 wins, not five. Losses by four to Philadelphia, five to the Giants, six at Baltimore and three to Cleveland could have gone the other way. Net EPA still ranks 29th, though, so this is a bad team that has been unlucky, not a good team hiding behind its record.

The real progress is on defense. The last two seasons ended at 3 wins with defenses that gave up more than 27 points a game. This one allows 22.3, 15th in the league, while the offense ranks dead last in time of possession. The tackling is the foundation: a 4.6% missed-tackle rate is 2nd best. The coverage is the soft spot. Pass EPA allowed ranks 25th and explosive pass rate allowed 26th, and Cleveland's offense, ranked 24th, threw for 308 yards on them last week.

The last two games brought the season's two best scoring outputs, 26 and 24. Week 7 was also the only clearly positive passing game by EPA. That is a small, encouraging sample. It arrives just as the schedule turns to one of the league's most efficient pass offenses.

strengths.title: Sure tackling keeps plays contained
strengths.body: The defense misses tackles on just 4.6% of attempts, 2nd in the league. That is why points allowed sit mid-pack even though EPA allowed is poor and the defense is on the field constantly. Tackling is a repeatable skill, so this should hold. It also limits how far the coverage problems can snowball into long touchdowns.

strengths.title: Pass protection is not the problem
strengths.body: Ward is rarely hit: the line ranks 4th in QB-hit rate allowed and 8th in sack rate. It also avoids negative runs, with a stuff rate that ranks 6th. The front is functional enough that the offensive struggles trace back to the receiving and decision-making layer. That makes the line one of the more stable pieces to build around.

strengths.title: Pass rush that can swing games
strengths.body: 17 sacks rank 11th, and the one win came on a six-sack, three-takeaway day at Indianapolis. The pressure rate itself is only 22nd, so the sacks are more opportunistic than dominant. The rush is good enough to produce a game-wrecking afternoon now and then, but not to count on weekly.

concerns.title: A passing game that can't stretch anything
concerns.body: Offensive pass EPA ranks 29th, and the overall offense is 31st in EPA and last in yards. Ward has 1,179 passing yards through seven starts. The run-heavy tendency (30th in pass rate over expected) protects him, but it also caps scoring when the team falls behind. This is the core flaw, not a cost of the strategy.

concerns.title: Coverage leaks explosives and short gains
concerns.body: Pass EPA allowed ranks 25th. The defense is poor both underneath (short EPA 26th) and on chunk plays (explosive pass rate 26th). Good tackling limits the damage after the catch, but quarterbacks are completing the throws. Against pass-first offenses, this is how the Titans get separated.

concerns.title: Turnovers in a margin-thin offense
concerns.body: The offense has 10 giveaways against 7 takeaways and has coughed it up in every game but one. For a team that wins only by keeping scores low, giving away possessions erases its whole plan. Some of that is variance, but an inefficient passing offense tends to keep producing it.

trend.note: The offense bottomed out with three points against Houston, then scored a season-high 26 at Indianapolis and 24 against Cleveland. Meanwhile the defense gave up its worst yardage day in the loss to the Browns. The arrow on offense is tentatively up, but the results swing week to week.

nextGame.headline: A run-first underdog against the league's most pass-happy offense
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati ranks 3rd in net EPA and 1st in pass rate over expected. It throws more than anyone in neutral situations, and it is about to face a Titans pass defense ranked 25th. The Bengals' defense pairs the league's most sacks with a strong deep-ball defense. It is vulnerable in the short game (30th), on third down (30th) and with missed tackles (29th). The Book has Tennessee as a 10-point underdog at +440 with a total of 46.5, well above any Titans game so far. The road to an upset runs through patience: short completions, Pollard carries and drives that end in points.

Tennessee will be without WR Calvin Ridley (hip) and RB Tyjae Spears (knee). Spears' absence pushes even more of the backfield onto Pollard and removes a receiving option out of the backfield. Punter Tommy Townsend is questionable with a knee injury, which matters for a team that needs field position. LB Dorian Mausi's practice window is open, but he has not played. For Cincinnati, Joe Burrow has started every game. Safety Kyle Dugger is out, but he was a part-time player. The bigger hole is at tight end, where Tanner Hudson is on IR and Erick All Jr. is questionable.

waysToWin.title: Live underneath, move the chains
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati is 30th in short-pass EPA allowed, 29th in missed tackles and 30th on third down. Quick throws to Wan'Dale Robinson and Gunnar Helm attack that directly and get the ball out before the league's top sack total can matter. The Bengals also rank 30th against tight ends, a real opening for Helm.

waysToWin.title: Shorten the game and steal possessions
waysToWin.body: Bleeding clock with Pollard and staying aggressive on fourth down keeps Burrow on the sideline in a game the Titans want in the teens. Cincinnati allows a lot of explosive runs (25th), so the run game has some upside here.

waysToWin.title: Hit Burrow and take the ball
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati's line ranks 26th in QB-hit rate allowed, and the Titans' best day came when they sacked Indianapolis six times and forced three turnovers. A couple of hits leading to a takeaway or a short field is the most realistic way a big underdog closes the gap.

waysToLose.title: Burrow picks apart the coverage
waysToLose.body: A top-6 pass offense that throws more than anyone meets a defense ranked 26th in explosive passes allowed and 26th underneath. Cleveland threw for 308 yards last week. Cincinnati can do more with the same openings, and early scoring wrecks the Titans' low-possession plan.

waysToLose.title: Chasing points into the sack leader
waysToLose.body: If Tennessee falls behind, it has to drop back against the league's 2nd-best sack rate. That is the Houston script: four sacks, two turnovers and three points. The Bengals' 10 takeaways rank 7th, and Ward has to be careful in obvious passing downs.

waysToLose.title: Drives that die in the red zone
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati allows touchdowns on just 35% of red-zone trips, 3rd best. An offense that already struggles to finish can move the ball and still come away with field goals, which isn't enough against a team scoring 27.2 a game.

nextGame.watch: Whether Ward's quick game can keep winning third downs against a Bengals defense that is soft underneath but lethal once it gets to the quarterback.

restOfSeason.body:
Some of the close-game bad luck should even out. A team this competitive in one-score games rarely stays at a .200 clip, and the remaining slate has soft spots. Washington is 1-4-1, and Indianapolis, Houston and Las Vegas are all .500 or worse. Dallas and Detroit rank 30th and 31st on defense, which gives this offense its best chances to score. The defense's improvement over the last two years looks real because it rests on tackling and pass rush rather than turnover luck.

The ceiling is set by the passing game, though. Until it moves out of the bottom four, every win will need the defense to hold opponents near 20. Jacksonville twice, Detroit and Dallas bring top-5 offenses that can push past that. Expect a team that plays more close games and steals a few more of them. It still finishes near the bottom of the division and well short of the playoff race.
swingFactors: Whether the Week 7 passing uptick is real
Coverage holding up against top passing offenses

confidence.note: Seven games with a stable QB, but the close-loss record and recent offensive uptick rest on small samples.
